<reason>Both sides built a genuinely sophisticated exchange, but A's central "fork" — either earlier disclosure is a trivial screen-shift that changes nothing (since sunk browsing costs and zero financial commitment are identical at cart and payment), or it demands numbers that don't exist yet and forces worst-case anchors/folded prices — was never cleanly escaped. B's best counter-move, "conditional itemized disclosure" (a menu policy like "18% for parties of 6+"), was clever but A correctly exposed it as a fee schedule rather than disclosure of an actual charge, and it left the app/ticketing "ambush" scenario from B's own opening untouched. B's anchoring/switching-cost mechanism is intuitively strong and well-grounded in real checkout psychology, but B never rebutted A's sharpest logical jab — that if recalibration at the cart screen defeats anchoring, the same recalibration logic should apply at payment, since neither screen involves any money actually moving. A also had the last word and used it precisely to answer B's clever closing reframe ("neither horn is worse than the status quo, so the dilemma is a concession"), arguing the status quo already delivers the motion's stated goal before any dollar moves. That left B's most interesting late argument unrebutted only because B could not reply further, while A's argumentative structure remained standing through both rebuttal rounds and the close.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's dilemma in Rebuttal 2 ([A4.3]-[A4.4]) — that PRO's own anchoring logic requires recalibration to work at the cart but fail at payment, when both are equally "before money moves" — was the most damaging unanswered pressure point of the debate.</best_rebuttal>
